title: Does buffering with NaHCO3 or TRIS buffer affect blood coagulation? A ROTEM study
summary:
This study aims to investigate how two drugs used to treat hyperacidity of the blood (metabolic acidosis) affect blood clotting. A pH value that is too low in the blood can disrupt many important bodily functions, as numerous enzymatic processes are pH-dependent. Such acidosis occurs frequently, especially in intensive care patients. Among other things, it has been observed that drugs such as norepinephrine are less effective in such cases. For this reason, buffer solutions are administered in cases of severe acidosis in order to raise the pH level again.
Clinically, sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO₃) and TRIS buffer are primarily used. Sodium bicarbonate acts via the body's own carbonic acid-bicarbonate buffer system, but can increase sodium levels in the blood and lead to increased formation of CO₂, which must be exhaled via the lungs. The TRIS buffer does not have these disadvantages, as it produces neither additional sodium nor CO₂. Nevertheless, it is used comparatively rarely.
Observations from military medical evaluations and experimental laboratory studies suggest that TRIS buffer may influence blood clotting by hindering the formation of stable fibrin structures. This could explain why treated patients required more blood transfusions and needed to remain in intensive care for longer.
The hypothesis of the planned study is therefore that the TRIS buffer has a measurable effect on blood clotting, while sodium bicarbonate does not have this effect. This will be systematically investigated using a ROTEM analysis.
